title: Delhi High Court: A GST Show Cause Notice Is Issued Only When the Taxpayer Can See It, Not When an Officer Generates It
meta_description: Delhi High Court quashes a GST demand against a Gurugram dealership, holding a notice generated in time but uploaded late to the portal is time-barred.
case_name: Sikka Motors Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India & Anr.
body: A limitation question that keeps coming up for businesses across Delhi NCR dealing with GST notices has a clearer answer after a Delhi High Court ruling delivered on 27 October 2026. The court held, in Sikka Motors Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India & Anr., that a show cause notice under the CGST Act counts as issued only when it reaches the taxpayer, not when a tax officer generates it on the department's internal system.

The petitioner, a Hyundai dealership, was contesting a demand relating to financial year 2019-20. According to the reports of the judgment, the show cause notice was generated within the statutory period but became visible on the GST portal only after that period had already run out, and the eventual demand order was passed relying on that notice. The dealership argued that the department could not extend its own limitation simply by generating a document internally while keeping it from the taxpayer until later.

That argument succeeded. The court read Section 73(2) of the CGST Act, which fixes how far in advance of the final adjudication deadline a show cause notice must be issued, together with Section 169, which lists the modes through which a notice can be validly served, including upload on the common portal. On that reading, generation of a notice inside the department's system is an internal administrative step, not service. The clock on the taxpayer's limitation protection runs from the date the notice actually becomes available to the taxpayer through one of the modes Section 169 recognises, and a notice that only becomes visible after the limitation period has expired cannot retroactively validate a demand built on it.

It also rejected the suggestion that a prior scrutiny communication in Form ASMT-10, or an opportunity for a personal hearing given later in the process, could substitute for a validly and timely served show cause notice. A scrutiny communication flags discrepancies for a response; it is not the formal notice that triggers adjudication under Section 73, and procedural fairness at a later stage does not cure a notice that was already out of time when it was actually served.

On this basis, the court quashed both the show cause notice and the demand order that followed from it, bringing the proceeding against the dealership to an end on the limitation point without going into the merits of the alleged input tax credit discrepancy that had triggered the notice in the first place.

The ruling sits within a wider and still unsettled area of GST litigation around portal mechanics. Several High Courts, including the Delhi High Court in earlier matters, have dealt with disputes over notices uploaded to a hidden or less visible section of the GST portal, service by email where the taxpayer disputes having seen it, and discrepancies between a notice's internal generation date and its public availability date. A separate, larger question, over the validity of government notifications that extended adjudication timelines during and after the pandemic, is pending before the Supreme Court and has caused several High Courts to keep related limitation challenges on hold pending that outcome. The Sikka Motors ruling does not touch that pending question; it turns on the narrower point of when a notice is treated as served, which the court resolved without needing to wait for the Supreme Court's ruling on the notification challenge.

For businesses operating in Delhi NCR, where a large share of GST adjudication for traders and dealerships runs through this High Court's jurisdiction, the practical lesson is to track two dates separately: the date stamped on a notice, and the date it actually becomes accessible through the portal, registered email or another recognised mode. Where those two dates sit on opposite sides of a limitation deadline, the gap itself can be a ground to challenge the notice, independent of whatever is alleged on the merits.

The judgment does not disturb the department's ability to issue notices and complete adjudication within time. It only confirms that the statutory clock is measured by when a taxpayer could reasonably know a notice exists, not by an internal system log that the taxpayer never sees until after the fact.
why_it_matters: GST portal delays and glitches are common, and this ruling gives taxpayers a concrete limitation defence when a notice is generated on time internally but only reaches them after the statutory window has closed. Businesses facing a GST demand should check the gap between a notice's generation date and its actual portal visibility or service date, since that gap can by itself be a ground to have the notice and any resulting order quashed.
card_summary: Delhi High Court quashed a GST demand against a dealership, holding a notice generated on time but visible on the portal only after limitation expired is time-barred, whatever its internal generation date.
card_tip: Compare a GST notice's internal generation date with when it actually became visible to you; a notice served past the Section 73(2) deadline can be time-barred even if drafted earlier.
verification_notes: Selected because GST notice and limitation disputes are a consistently high-search tax topic for Delhi NCR businesses, and this is a fresh, clearly dated ruling (27 October 2026) not yet covered on the site; the existing blog guide on GST show cause notices covers natural justice defects generally, not this specific portal-timing limitation point. Case name, W.P.(C) 5076/2025, and the 27 October 2026 date are confirmed across three independent reports (Taxscan, LiveLaw Biz, StudyCafe). The bench composition (reported in one source as Justices Anil Kshetarpal and Bharat Parashar) could not be confirmed in a second independent source, so it is described here only as a Division Bench. The exact show cause notice and portal-upload dates reported (generated before the FY2019-20 deadline, uploaded in August 2024) vary slightly between sources and are therefore described only in general terms rather than with specific dates.
